subject: Cognitive Science
title: Means-Ends Analysis
description: Learn Means-Ends Analysis in one minute.

hook.text: You're in city A. Goal: reach city Z. Means-ends analysis says: find the biggest gap and close it first.

buildup.text: It's a general strategy: compare current state to goal state, identify differences, reduce the biggest one.

discovery.text: Newell and Simon built it into their General Problem Solver in 1957—one of AI's earliest programs.

twist.text: Sometimes the right move increases the gap temporarily. Means-ends analysis can miss indirect solutions.

climax.text: GPS showed that many human problem-solving strategies reduce to this single gap-closing loop.

punchline.text: Find the gap. Close the gap. Repeat.

quiz.question: What is means-ends analysis?
options: Reducing the biggest difference between current and goal state
Working only from the goal backward

details.summary: Means-ends analysis breaks the gap between current state and goal state into smaller subproblems. At each step, you identify the biggest difference between where you are and where you want to be, then find an action to reduce that difference. GPS, the first AI reasoning program, used this strategy.
details.whyItMatters: Means-ends analysis is a universal problem-solving strategy that works across domains. It is how most people naturally approach complex, multi-step problems.
takeaways: Compare current state to goal state and reduce the difference
Break large problems into manageable subgoals
The strategy works across many different problem domains

faq.question: When does means-ends analysis fail?
faq.answer: It fails when solving a problem requires temporarily moving away from the goal, increasing the distance before you can decrease it. People resist moves that seem to make things worse even when they are necessary steps. Problems requiring detours are systematically harder for means-ends analysis.

faq.question: How does means-ends analysis relate to AI?
faq.answer: Newell and Simon's General Problem Solver in 1957 was one of the first AI programs and used means-ends analysis. Modern AI has moved beyond it, but the principle of decomposing problems into subgoals remains fundamental to both human and artificial problem-solving approaches.
